+@F4@ This is where the account of printing becomes an account of further finishing. +@F5@ Now the essay has moved from the edition to a named institution's copy. That move needs to be announced. The household accounts, the promises of payment, the small disputes preserved in careful columns: these were things a person could explain saving. Her brother carried a blanket tied around a collection of objects whose shapes she could not identify. He had refused to open it for inspection. Now they stood outside the room they had rented, waiting for each other to decide which direction counted as away. Neither wanted to admit that the other might know.

+Ada had brought the letter in a pocket where her brother could not see it. She had folded it so often that the paper seemed prepared to come apart along the same narrow lines. +
+@F2@ Ada kept repeating the park's name to herself as though it might help her remember the route back. Will trusted signs and the visible movement of other visitors. +

+
+@F5@ Will liked the number. He said it twice, once to her and once almost under his breath, as though the second saying might make the height more available to the imagination. +The coat had been hanging behind the door so long that I had stopped seeing the missing button as damage. It was simply the shape of the coat: a dark front, an empty place, a loose thread that caught on my fingernail when I reached into the pocket. I wore it on days when I did not expect anyone to look closely. That was most days, until my sister asked why I kept holding it shut with one hand. I told her I liked having something to do with my hand. She waited for the better answer.
+
+@N1@ I remember the year because I had written it on the paper bag, as if a bag were a receipt for the person I hoped to become. The coat was more formal than anything else I owned. I imagined entering rooms with less apology simply because the shoulders sat differently. In practice I carried the same hesitant person inside it. The coat did not object. It acquired my habit of being dropped over chairs, my small pocket collections, and a pale mark near the cuff that I could never quite explain.
+
+My sister brought a tin of spare buttons when she came for dinner. She set it beside the bread without presenting it as a solution, which made me suspicious. I wanted to say that I had not asked for a repair service. Instead I opened the lid. There were buttons that looked like sweets, buttons so small I could barely hold them, a pair still joined by a loop of thread. None matched the remaining buttons on the coat. I felt an immediate, disproportionate relief. The sensible thing could not be done exactly, so perhaps nothing needed to be done.
+
+She chose a dark one and put it on the table. I said it was wrong. She agreed, then asked whether wrong meant unusable. I disliked the question because I could hear myself asking it in another context, with the confidence of someone advising a person whose difficulty was not her own. Here the distinction felt less generous. I wanted the repair to restore an earlier version of the coat, and the mismatched button announced that the earlier version was unavailable. My sister went to wash her hands, leaving the choice in front of me.
+
+@N2@ It was an estimate of feeling, not of pressure on the fabric. I could still put my thumb against the empty place and pull the edges together, but the gesture now seemed to admit something I had been trying to postpone. I did not want a new coat. I did not particularly want this coat improved. I wanted to stop being asked what the missing button meant. The wish was unreasonable, but recognizing that did not make it disappear. I sat with the tin open and tried not to turn my reluctance into a theory about everyone else.
+
+After dinner, my sister asked for thread. I showed her the drawer, then regretted it when she found the packet I had bought for this exact purpose months before. She did not mention the packet's unopened state. Her silence was more effective than an accusation would have been. I could imagine defending myself against criticism. I could not defend myself against a person quietly arranging a needle, a spool, and a coat on the cleared end of the table. She asked whether I wanted to do it. I said that I did, though I had not known it until she asked.
+
+The needle seemed too small for the amount of thought I had given the problem. I held it toward the lamp and missed the eye twice. My sister moved the breadbasket out of the way. There was something comforting about the lack of ceremony. Nobody said that mending was a lesson, or that I would feel better when the task was finished. I was allowed to be clumsy at a small action without having the clumsiness stand for a defect in my character. When the thread finally passed through, I felt pleased in a way that did not require explanation.
+
+@N3@ I had been treating the missing piece as evidence that the whole thing belonged to a completed part of my life. The mismatched replacement made another possibility visible. I could continue wearing something without pretending that continuation meant restoration. This was a thought about my coat, at my table. I did not want to enlarge it into advice for people facing losses I had no right to compare with a button. Its usefulness depended on its smallness. It gave me a way to finish the task without claiming to have understood more than I had.
+
+When I stood up, the coat closed unevenly. I had placed the new button slightly higher than I intended. My sister looked at it and said nothing. I was grateful, then annoyed by the gratitude, then amused by the effort required to accept help without turning it into an account of my independence. I asked whether she thought it should move. She said she thought I should try wearing it first. That answer left the decision with me while saving me from making it at once. I put the needle away before I could reopen the argument.
+
+@N4@ The next morning I walked out with both hands in my pockets. I noticed the difference immediately and then forgot it until I reached the corner. The button had not changed the day. It had removed a small task I had mistaken for part of my nature. Later, hanging the coat behind the door, I looked at the new dark circle and the older ones beside it. The mismatch was visible if I looked. I decided that looking did not oblige me to undo anything. Then I closed the door, and the coat disappeared behind it as usual.

+I found the postcard while looking for a battery. It had slipped beneath a stack of envelopes, picture side down, so that the first thing I saw was my own unfinished sentence. The handwriting looked impatient. I had begun too close to the top and left an extravagant amount of space beneath the words, as though the difficult part would be finding room for all I intended to say. Instead the difficult part had been continuing. I put the card on the table and forgot about the battery until the clock stopped within earshot.
+
+@N1@ I do not remember the shop where I bought it. I remember carrying it back in a pocket that was too shallow, and pressing it flat beneath a book before trying to write. The picture had seemed suitable because it gave me something to mention before reaching the actual purpose of the message. I could describe the weather in the image, the color of a doorway, the angle from which the street had been photographed. Anything that let me approach my sister indirectly felt, at the time, like a useful beginning.
+
+The sentence stopped after the word perhaps. I had disliked that word even while writing it. It gave me somewhere to hide a request I was not yet ready to state. Perhaps we could talk; perhaps I had misunderstood; perhaps enough time had passed for neither of us to remember the precise shape of the argument. Each version asked the other person to do a different kind of work. I had not decided which work I was entitled to ask for. The card went into an envelope without an address, and the envelope eventually became part of the drawer.
+
+@N2@ The count surprised me because I had thought of the collection as an accident rather than a habit. Some cards were blank. One carried a shopping list. Another had a name crossed out so firmly that I could not tell whether I had changed the recipient or simply the spelling. I laid them in a row and immediately disliked the display. It made the drawer look like evidence in a case I was building against myself. I put all but the unfinished card away. One awkward object was enough company for the afternoon.
+
+I made tea and took the card to the window. The picture looked duller than I remembered, though that may have been the light or my expectation of it. I wanted an image dramatic enough to justify having kept it. Instead there was an ordinary street and a patch of sky cut off by the edge. The modesty of the picture began to seem helpful. I did not need the card to represent an entire journey. It could remain something I had bought because I wanted to send a few words and had not managed to choose them.
+
+My sister and I had spoken many times since then. We had discussed work, meals, an inconvenient train, a shelf she was trying to put up. The old argument did not stand between every sentence. That made the unfinished message harder to understand. Was it still waiting to be sent, or was it only a record of a person who had once needed to write it? I could not tell whether keeping it was tenderness toward that person or an excuse for avoiding a decision. The question grew less useful the longer I tried to make it answer itself.
+
+@N3@ I was thinking about the ease with which I could invent a second person who would finally know what the first one meant. A future version of me would complete the sentence elegantly, put a stamp on the envelope, and feel no doubt about whether it should travel. The actual person at the window had a cold cup of tea and a pencil with a broken point. I found those limitations unexpectedly reassuring. They were specific enough to work with. I could sharpen the pencil. I did not have to solve the entire history of my hesitation first.
+
+On another piece of paper, I wrote the sentence I would use now. It was shorter and less graceful than the old opening. It asked whether my sister wanted to walk with me on Sunday. I had to stop myself from adding an explanation about the card. The explanation would have made the invitation answer for more than it needed to. I wanted to offer an hour together, not present an object and ask her to confirm my account of its significance. The difference seemed important enough to keep, though I could not have defended it in a tidy paragraph.
+
+I sent the invitation in a message and left the card on the table. For a while I felt that I had cheated by choosing an easier form. Then I noticed that the feeling depended on imagining the difficult form as automatically more sincere. I did not know why I had granted it that authority. Paper could hold evasion as easily as a screen. That was a judgment about my own unfinished sentence, not a conclusion about how other people should communicate. I let the card remain an object whose failure did not have to invalidate the invitation.
+
+@N4@ When my sister replied, she asked whether we could walk later in the day. I said yes. The exchange was practical and entirely adequate to the question I had actually asked. I returned the card to the drawer, this time without an envelope. I did not finish the sentence or cross it out. I put the new battery in the clock and listened to it resume. The small sound made the room feel occupied again. There was nothing ceremonious left to do, which was a relief I had not known how to request.

+On her first morning at the archive, Leila was given a box of papers and asked to describe it before moving anything. The request sounded unnecessarily cautious. The papers were uneven, some envelopes were empty, and the folders did not match. She could make the box look better in a few minutes. The supervisor asked her to wait. An arrangement that appears untidy can still carry information about how its owner used it, and the first task was to preserve an account of what had arrived.
+
+@A@
+
+The number belongs in the record because it lets the next volunteer check whether the contents have changed. The name identifies the person responsible for the observation. Neither detail needs to be made dramatic. A useful record should be ordinary enough to read quickly and precise enough to answer a later question. If the description says only that several folders were received, someone will eventually have to decide whether several means the same number that is now on the shelf.
+
+@B@
+
+The rule does not mean that a volunteer must preserve every accidental crease or refuse to remove a dangerous staple. It means that a change should be considered and recorded, rather than made invisible by a desire for neatness. If the reason for a grouping is unclear, stop and ask. Do not supply a confident explanation because the form appears to require one. A note that says the purpose is unknown is more useful than a guess that later readers cannot distinguish from something the donor actually told us.
+
+Descriptions should separate observation from inference. A folder labeled with a street name can be described that way. It should not automatically be described as a property file unless the contents or the donor establish that use. The label may refer to a person, a project, or a visit. You do not have to solve every puzzle on arrival. You do need to leave a record that makes clear which parts you saw and which parts remain questions for someone with more time or context.
+
+When the intake is complete, put the box in the assigned temporary location and enter that location in the register.
